judgment.rationale: B4.4.1.1 (Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1: Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis) asks learners to demonstrate understanding of many-to-one correspondence in displaying and reading/interpreting graphs; B4.2.1.3 (Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 1: Patterns and Relationships) asks learners to represent, describe and extend patterns and relationships using charts and tables to solve problems. Both are BASIC 4 Content Standards (rank 0, same grain) and share substantive coherence in organising and reading information in tabular/graphical representations, so mutual reinforcement across data handling and algebraic pattern representation is meaningful. However, neither statement's evidence shows that proficiency in one supports success in the other: graph scale/many-to-one correspondence and pattern extension in charts are distinct skill targets in different strands, and same-rank developmental direction is not substantiated. Symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment; the shared 'Basic 4' ancestor, weak code-prefix overlap ('b4'), and generic token overlap ('and', 'to') were treated as nomination signals only. Evidence is bounded: both endpoints' source evidence is truncated (32 and 24 omitted items) and no Learning Components were supplied.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 (rank 2) Indicators in Strand 4: Data, Sub-strand 1 (Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis), but sit under different Content Standards: B6.4.1.1 (create, label and interpret line graphs) for the first and B6.4.1.2 (select, justify and use appropriate data-collection methods) for the second. B6.4.1.1.2 asks learners to judge whether a data set is continuous (line graph) or discrete (series of points) and explain why; B6.4.1.2.1 asks learners to select a data-collection method for a given question and justify the choice (LCs: 'select a method for collecting data to answer a given question', 'justify the choice of data collection method'). These are complementary phases of the same statistical enquiry cycle, sharing a reasoning/justification demand about data type and purpose, but neither statement's content is a demonstrated precondition for the other and both share the same grade rank with no substantive evidence of developmental ordering, so a symmetric relatesTo is the supported judgment rather than buildsTowards. Shared ancestors, code prefix and token overlap ('data', 'given') alone were not treated as sufficient evidence. judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 5 (rank 1) Indicators of the same grain sharing Content Standard B5.1.4.1 ('Demonstrate understanding of decimals fractions and strategies for comparing, adding and subtracting decimal fraction'). B5.1.4.1.2 requires comparing and ordering decimal fractions to the thousandths with <, >, =, establishing decimal place-value magnitude and relative-position judgment; B5.1.4.1.3 requires rounding decimals to the nearest tenth and hundredth, which operationally depends on judging which benchmark value a decimal is nearer to. Proficiency in comparing/ordering decimals therefore supports success in rounding decimals, a substantive same-rank developmental direction rather than mere code adjacency or page proximity. Note that shared-parent, code-prefix and page-gap nominations alone were not treated as semantic evidence, and both endpoints carry unresolved-ancestry and truncated source-evidence limitations, so the judgment rests on the trustworthy statement texts and resolved BASIC 5 coordinates.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 4 Indicators (same coordinate rank 0) in Strand 2: Algebra, Sub-strand 2: Unknowns, Expressions and Equations, so the grain and domain match. First (B4.2.2.1.1) requires writing a given problem as an equation in which a symbol represents an unknown number; second (B4.2.2.2.4) requires solving a given one-step equation by 'guess and check' under Content Standard B4.2.2.2 'Solve one-step equations involving a symbol to represent an unknown number'. Beyond shared wording, there is substantive same-rank developmental evidence: fluency in representing an unknown by a symbol within an equation is the formulation skill on which the solving indicator operates, since guess-and-check requires interpreting the symbol as an unknown value to be found. This supports likelihood of success rather than strict prerequisite ordering, hence buildsTowards from the representation indicator to the solving indicator. Judgment is bounded by truncated source evidence (24 omitted items per endpoint) and upstream audit/merge context on both endpoints and their ancestors.

judgment.rationale: Both are BASIC 6 Indicators (same rank 2) under Strand 1: Number, but sit in different sub-strands: B6.1.3.1.3 (Sub-Strand 3: Fractions) asks learners to use models to explain multiplying a fraction by a whole number, a whole number by a fraction, and a fraction by a fraction, while B6.1.2.1.2 (Sub-Strand 2: Number Operations) asks learners to apply mental mathematics strategies for multiplication (annexing then adding zero, halving and doubling, the distributive property). Same-grade, same-strand proximity and shared code prefix alone are not treated as developmental evidence. B5.4.2.1.1 establishes the qualitative chance vocabulary by classifying a single outcome in a probability experiment as impossible, possible, or certain. B5.4.2.1.3 (LCs: conduct a given probability experiment a number of times; record the outcomes; explain the results) is substantively more complex: it combines repeated experimentation, systematic recording, and explanation of empirical results, which draws on the classification language established in .1 to interpret and justify observed outcomes. Same-rank direction is therefore supported by this specific increase in complexity and by the dependence of the explanatory work on prior likelihood classification, not merely by shared parent, code prefix, page proximity, or token overlap. judgment.rationale: Same-grain Indicator pair, both resolved to BASIC 5 (rank 1), both direct children of Content Standard B5.2.1.1 'Determine the pattern rule to make predictions about subsequent elements' within Strand 2 Algebra, Sub-strand 1 Patterns and Relationships. First (B5.2.1.1.6) requires determining and explaining why a given number is or is not the next element in a pattern (LCs split into a 'determine whether' component and an 'explain why' component tagged reasoning); second (B5.2.1.1.4) requires representing a given pattern visually to verify predictions (LC tagged pattern/predictions/visual representation). These are complementary skills for the same pattern-rule goal: one supplies a visual representation used to check predicted continuations, the other evaluates and justifies a specific candidate continuation. Neither subsumes or escalates the other, and the bounded evidence gives no pair-specific indication that proficiency in the visual-representation indicator increases likelihood of success in the explain-why indicator (or vice versa) beyond a generic cognitive argument; the direction is genuinely symmetric, so same-rank buildsTowards is not justified. The coherence is nonetheless substantive and pair-specific rather than mere shared wording ('a', 'given', 'pattern'), shared ancestry, or code prefix, all of which were discounted, so canonical relatesTo with null direction is the correct judgment. Limitations: both endpoints carry upstream audit/merge/code context and truncated source evidence (24 omitted items each), so exemplar detail that might sharpen the relationship was unavailable.
